title: The sleeping giant NGC 4889
caption: The elliptical galaxy NGC 4889, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: NGC 4889 · constellation Coma Berenices · about 300 million light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: Official ESA/Hubble press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: The elliptical galaxy NGC 4889 sits in front of hundreds of background galaxies in this Hubble image, deep inside the Coma galaxy cluster. It lies about 300 million light-years away in the constellation Coma Berenices.

An elliptical galaxy is a smooth, rounded collection of stars without the arms or flat disc of a spiral. From the outside, NGC 4889 looks calm, set against hundreds of galaxies that lie much farther away.

Well out of sight of human eyes, a gigantic supermassive black hole sits at the galaxy's center. A supermassive black hole is an object so dense that not even light escapes it, and such objects are thought to lie at the hearts of most large galaxies. This one cannot be seen at all, and its presence is known from its effects rather than from any light it gives off.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (3.23 x 2.15 arcminutes) and distance (300 million light years), the frame spans roughly 282,000 × 188,000 light-years. Its light set out about 300 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, using a blue filter and a near-infrared filter. The source does not publish which color was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: The black hole is invisible in any light, and part of this data is near-infrared light the eye cannot see.
